transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-06-09 14:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Evelyn Park (Redwood AE), Marcus Li (Redwood SE), Janelle Ortiz (AtlasHead of Platform), Ravi Menon (Infra), Sofia Alvarez (Security)

[00:00] Evelyn: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick note, Marcus and I will run through the on-prem artifact and driver workflow, then we can dig into any perf questions, ok?
[00:17] Janelle: Yep, thanks. We're particularly keen on the offline licensing side and how you deliver the GPU driver bundles — our data center is air-gapped so networking is, uh, limited.
[00:29] Marcus: Totally understood. We'll show the bundle pattern we use: compressed tarball with signed manifest, sha256 sums, and an installation checklist. For air-gapped installs we support a transfer package and an offline license token exchange — basically a signed license blob exchanged by your operator.
[00:47] Ravi: Quick question, what about NVIDIA driver compatibility matrix? we run mixed gen cards — A100s and some A30s — and for some hosts, our ops team is strict about kernel modules.
[01:02] Marcus: Good q. We produce driver bundles per CUDA driver version + kernel module build notes. For A100/A30 we recommend NVIDIA driver >= 525 with the matching CUDA 11/12 toolkit; we'll include a per-card compatibility file. There is a small caveat: if your kernels are custom, you might need to compile the nvidia module on host — we include a build script and instructions.
[01:27] Sofia: And from a security angle, how are the artifacts validated and how do we verify integrity post-transfer? hashes only or signed?
[01:35] Marcus: Both. The tar includes a manifest.json and we sign the manifest with Redwood's private key. We provide the public key in the transfer pack so your ops can verify signatures offline. Hashes (sha256) are included for each binary and for the manifest as well.
[01:50] Evelyn: Also note the offline license token uses asymmetric signing and is time-bounded; you can pin the validity window. We'll share the exact token format in the licensing doc.
[02:02] Janelle: Sounds good. On the runtime perf side, our main concerns are latency for 1–2k QPS at small batch sizes and kv cache behaviour across long-lived chat sessions.
[02:15] Marcus: Ok, performance layers: kernel/driver correctness first, then quant and batching. For low-latency small-batch traffic we typically advise single-request fast path — low batching, reduced context prefetching, and warm KV cache. For throughput bursts you enable dynamic batching with a 5–15ms aggregation window.
[02:39] Ravi: When you say KV cache warm, are you doing prefix caching across requests or per-connection? we need to understand memory usage and eviction.
[02:50] Marcus: It's per-model worker KV cache keyed by request prefix hashes; cache entries are shared across sessions on the same worker if the prefix matches. Eviction is LRU with a configurable max-entries and estimated memory cap. We'll include sample defaults (e.g., 10k entries -> ~6GB for a 70B model's KVs) and guidance for tuning.
[03:14] Sofia: Can Redwood integrate with our KMS/HSM for key wrap of offline license keys? we can't store plaintext tokens on the transfer media.
[03:24] Evelyn: Yes; we support wrapping the license blob with a customer-supplied public key. For HSM integration on-prem we can do an exchange where your HSM signs a CSR and we encrypt the license using the resulting public key. We'll need your security team to confirm supported algorithms.
[03:42] Sofia: We'll follow up with the algorithm list.
[03:46] Janelle: Back to drivers — what's the rollback story if a driver install causes a node fail? our ops are cautious about driver upgrades.
[03:56] Marcus: We include a staged install script: it creates a snapshot of current modules and can revert to previous driver and kernel module. We also recommend testing on a non-prod host first. For air-gapped installs we provide a restore package and an explicit rollback command.
[04:12] Ravi: For benchmarking, what artifacts do you need from us? GPU telemetry, kernel version, sample prompts?
[04:20] Marcus: Yes: GPU model + driver version, kernel version, CUDA/cuDNN versions, available RAM, and a set of representative prompts. If you can provide an SSH to a test VM we'll run short microbenchmarks (latency p50/p95 and throughput with batching).
[04:36] Janelle: We can provision a dev VM. Ravi will take that action.
[04:40] Ravi: Yeah I'll set that up; I'll need the install checklist first.
[04:43] Evelyn: We'll send it today. Marcus — anything else on quantization?
[04:47] Marcus: Sure — for latency we typically use 4-bit or 8-bit quant for 70B models depending on acceptable quality delta. We provide quant profiles as part of the artifact set and recommend A/B testing. Note that quant affects KVs and memory profiles; we include memory/cost estimates in the profile.
[05:07] Sofia: Any concerns about side-channel leakage in quantized kernels? our security team will ask.
[05:12] Marcus: We don't have customer-reported side-channel incidents; our kernels run with standard isolation, and we can provide kernel-level mitigations and recommended cgroup settings. We'll add a short note for you.
[05:25] Janelle: On networking, since we're air-gapped, how do you handle license renewals? periodic online check-ins won't work.
[05:33] Evelyn: We support time-bounded offline licenses. For renewals, your operator requests a renewal token from Redwood by sending the previous license fingerprint and a signed entropy blob — offline via secure transfer. We do a one-time manual verification step if required.
[05:50] Ravi: What's the expected install time for the full stack (runtime + drivers + model weights)? large weights take a while to transfer in our environment.
[05:58] Marcus: Transfer time is dominated by model weights; we provide delta bundles and chunked transfers so you can resume. For install itself (once files are local) about 15–30 minutes for runtime + drivers on a node depending on compilation steps; model load time varies by model size and NVMe speed.
[06:18] Janelle: Ok, good. Anything outstanding?
[06:22] Sofia: I want the signed manifest and hashing process in writing, plus the algorithm list for HSM wrap.
[06:28] Evelyn: We'll attach both in the licensing pack.
[06:31] Marcus: I'll produce the driver bundle and the install/rollback checklist + sha256 file. I'll also include a minimal systemd unit suggestion for auto-start and healthchecks.
[06:44] Ravi: I'll share the dev VM creds after I provision it.
[06:47] Evelyn: Great, recap: Evelyn sends licensing + SLA, Marcus sends driver bundle and hashes, Ravi provides VM, Sofia sends HSM/algorithm constraints. target dates in follow-up. Thanks everyone.
[06:58] Janelle: Thanks, appreciate the clear plan.
[07:01] Evelyn: We'll follow up with the artifacts and schedule the pilot.

End transcript.
